Meeting header:
2026-03-15 10:30 UTC • 62 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Reed (Redwood SE), Tori Lin (Redwood SE - joined 00:12), Priya K (NovaHealth - Head of ML), Ethan Park (Infra), Lena Morales (Security), Marco Silva (SRE)

Summary (auto):
High-level technical deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for NovaHealth's LLM inference workloads. Discussed burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs, KV cache warmup/priming, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: share pricing and benchmark artifacts; customer to share traffic traces for pilot sizing.

Topics (auto): autoscaling tuning; burst capacity and queueing; reserved vs on-demand GPUs; caching & warm start; batching and quantization; VPC/on-prem networking considerations.

00:00 - Alyssa: "All right hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — this is Alyssa from Redwood, Marcus is our SE. we'll go through autoscaling and capacity planning and leave time for questions. sound good?"
00:14 - Priya: "Yep all good — thanks. we are specifically trying to figure out how to handle our spikey traffic from charting and report generation, esp around release windows."
00:25 - Marcus: "Cool. a little context question first: what's your current stack and do you run in cloud VPC or on prem?"
00:33 - Ethan: "We run primarily in us-east k8s, EKS, some on-prem batch jobs in our colo. wanting to understand Redwood Dedicated vs Private options, and how we can reserve capacity for peak nights."
00:43 - Alyssa: "Right — Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput; Redwood Private is the VPC / on-prem option if you need more network isolation or compliance. for autoscaling we support both continuous autoscaling and fixed reserved pools with burst policies. we'll demo typical queueing models."
01:02 - Priya: "Can you explain burst policies — like what's the typical capacity you can burst to and how does billing work?"
01:10 - Marcus: "Sure. so our burst policy has two modes: queue-first and immediate-burst. queue-first keeps requests queued up to a threshold and prioritizes latency SLOs; immediate-burst will spin up extra nodes (if available) to keep latency low. bursting is limited by available pool capacity in the region or your reserved burst budget. billing is split — reserved capacity billed as a commit, burst usage billed at an overage rate. we'll send a cost example."
01:38 - Marco: "do you have hard limits on how fast you can spin up gpus? like cold start time? our concern is sudden 10x traffic for 2-3 minutes."
01:46 - Marcus: "Cold start for a new GPU is typically 60-180s depending on image pulls and kernel init; we reduce that with pre-warmed instances and snapshot images. for short spikes we recommend a combination: maintain a small pre-warm pool (eg 10% headroom) + config burst budget. also prefix KV cache warmup matters for latency on first requests."
02:12 - Priya: "KV cache — what's the best practice for warmup? we saw first-request P99s spike badly."
02:20 - Marcus: "Two patterns: proactive priming (run representative requests through cache when you boot nodes) and progressive lazy warmup (serve and backfill as requests hit). for chat-heavy workloads we keep a shared KV cache in Redis-like tier and mount local hot cache for immediate hits. note, cross-node KV consistency and sharding can add overhead."
03:00 - Ethan: "How do you model queueing? we need to give capacity numbers to finance and ops."
03:06 - Marcus: "We use a simple M/M/c inspired model as a starting place — arrival rate (lambda) from traces, service rate (mu) from microbenchmarks per model and sequence length, and c = number of concurrent GPU workers. we estimate P90/P99 latencies and then add headroom. Marcus: (laugh) there is a spreadsheet i'll share — it contains examples: single-model baseline, multi-model routing, and mixed sequence-length percentiles."
03:40 - Priya: "Can you account for batching? our workload has many short requests (avg 12 tokens) but a few long recaps (avg 400 tokens)."
03:48 - Marcus: "Batching reduces per-token cost but increases per-request latency. our runtime supports adaptive batching — it will batch compatible requests up to a max batch size or latency target. for many short requests, batching can drastically improve throughput and reduce GPUs needed; for long sequences you may want a dedicated worker pool or model variant. quantization also helps increase effective throughput per GPU."
04:20 - Priya: "About quantization — accuracy/regression risk? we are in healthcare domain so small hallucinations are risky."
04:26 - Marcus: "Yes, quantization is a trade-off. 8-bit often performs well for many open models; 4-bit is more aggressive and sometimes needs per-model evals. Redwood Optimize will recommend quant profiles and run A/B evals on your prompt set to track regressions. we typically run a QA eval suite during pilot."
05:00 - Lena: "From security: if we go Redwood Private in our VPC/on-prem, how are keys handled and do you support HSM/KMS?"
05:08 - Alyssa: "Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, network egress controls, and audit logs. we'll include our SOC2/ISO docs. there is a slight ops tradeoff — you'll manage some of the infra but get full control over keys and logs."
05:30 - Marco: "We heard about graceful degradation — what happens when capacity is exhausted?"
05:35 - Marcus: "We have fallback policies: route to lower-cost model variants, degrade non-critical endpoints, or queue with adaptive stepdown. we expose policy knobs: max queue time, drop thresholds, fallback models. recommends setting client-side timeouts and progressive degrade levels."
06:05 - Priya: "How to size reserved GPUs? we want a finance-approved number: committed for 3 months then scale."
06:12 - Marcus: "Start with core baseline to hit 95% of steady state traffic (from your traces). then add burst headroom (10-30% depending on historical spikes). for heavy bursty traffic you can commit to a smaller base and rely on burst budget. example: if you need 200 rps at P95 under average sequence length, microbenchmarks show a p4d can handle X tokens/sec when quantized — spreadsheet will show tokens/sec converted to rps. we'll model several scenarios."
06:50 - Priya: "Can we run a short POC with production traces?"
06:53 - Alyssa: "Absolutely — typical POC: 2 weeks, we run a pilot in your VPC or on Redwood Dedicated: 1) ingest traffic traces, 2) run benchmarks and queueing sims, 3) measure P95/P99 and cost, 4) produce a sizing recommendation and reserved quote. Marcus: we'll scope the pilot with SRE and infra — minimal token-level data but anonymized."
07:15 - Ethan: "What about cross-region failover? our DR requires region fallback with eventual consistency on KV caches."
07:22 - Marcus: "We support multi-region routing. for caches we recommend a cache tiering approach: local hot caches + global backing store; cross-region warmup on failover combined with gradual traffic shift. there will be a short spike on failover while KV warms up, plan headroom for that."
07:48 - Priya: "Any gotchas with on-prem GPU drivers and libs?"
07:52 - Tori: "Yes — driver mismatches and cuDNN/kernels are common pain points. our Private deployment includes an onboarding checklist: supported driver versions, container images, and testing harness. bring the driver versions we request or we can coordinate driver upgrades."
08:20 - Marco: "Do you support per-tenant isolation inside Dedicated? we might need tenant separation for PHI segments."
08:27 - Alyssa: "Yes, Dedicated offers pool-level isolation and RBAC. you can create dedicated clusters for PHI-handling routes and log access separately. we'll include a sample network diagram."
08:42 - Priya: "How do you instrument costs and attribute per-feature?"
08:45 - Marcus: "Redwood Console shows token-level cost breakdown, per-route/model dashboards, and tags for jobs so you can allocate cost by team. we can pipe cost exports to your billing system."
09:05 - Lena: "For compliance we'll need audit logs and SAML SSO — do you support SAML and audit retention settings?"
09:12 - Alyssa: "Yes, SAML/SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and configurable audit retention. Private allows you to keep logs in your own storage if required."
09:30 - Priya: "What do you need from us to run the sizing?"
09:33 - Marcus: "7 days of anonymized request traces with timestamps, model IDs, sequence length, and success/fail flags. if you can't share raw traces, aggregated percentiles and peak windows help too. also tell us which endpoints are critical vs optional."
09:55 - Priya: "We'll try to provide traces by Friday. Also want to understand cost per 1M tokens for reserved vs burst."
10:02 - Alyssa: "We'll include cost scenarios in the pricing doc. we'll show reserved commit amortized cost, overage rates, and example burst cost. action items and timeline we'll email after this call."
10:20 - (wrap) Alyssa: "Ok thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the benchmark sheet and next steps. any final questions?"
10:25 - Priya: "Nope that's it, thanks — appreciate the detail. we'll start pulling traces. bye."

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels are mostly accurate; occasional generic labels. Some product names slightly mis-transcribed (eg K V cache, Private spelled as private), typical of automated transcriptions.
